title: SQL
lead: Relational terminology, single-table queries, aggregation, joins and nested queries.
goals: Queries over multiple tables and joins

sections.title: Relational terminology and single-table queries
sections.html:
SQL is declarative: a query specifies the required result while the DBMS chooses an execution algorithm. DDL defines schemas, DML queries and modifies data, and DCL controls access. A relation has a schema of named, typed attributes and an instance of tuples. SQL normally uses bag semantics, allowing duplicate rows.

The source database contains Student(sid, name, dept, age), Enrolled(sid, cid, grade) and Course(cid, name, year). SELECT * FROM Student WHERE age = 18 keeps the students satisfying the predicate. SELECT chooses output expressions; DISTINCT removes duplicate output rows.

ORDER BY sorts by one or more expressions, using ASC or DESC for each. LIMIT restricts the number of output rows; OFFSET skips rows first. Without ORDER BY, the selected subset has no guaranteed order.

PDF pp. 1–12

sections.title: Aggregation, GROUP BY and HAVING
sections.html:
Aggregate functions summarise a collection of rows: COUNT counts, SUM sums, AVG averages, and MIN/MAX find extrema. GROUP BY partitions rows by the values of the grouping attributes and produces one aggregate result per group. In the standard grouped form taught here, a selected expression must be a grouping expression or an aggregate.

WHERE filters input rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregate values have been computed. The slide query SELECT dept, AVG(age) FROM Student GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(age) > 21 returns only departments whose average age exceeds 21.

The logical evaluation sequence is FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY/aggregation → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. It defines the query result; the optimiser may use another physical order when equivalence is preserved.

PDF pp. 13–18

sections.title: Queries over multiple tables and joins
sections.html:
A multi-table FROM clause conceptually forms a Cartesian product; the join predicate restricts it to matching pairs. The source query joins Student and Enrolled on sid and filters E.cid = 'INF-11199' to obtain names and grades. The DBMS can implement this without materialising the full product.

INNER JOIN returns matching pairs. NATURAL JOIN equates all attributes with matching names and retains one copy of each shared attribute, so its meaning depends on the schemas. Explicit JOIN ... ON makes the intended matching condition visible.

LEFT OUTER JOIN also preserves unmatched left rows, adding NULL values for the right attributes. RIGHT OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched right rows; FULL OUTER JOIN preserves both. A left row with several matching right rows still produces several result rows.

PDF pp. 19–25

sections.title: Nested queries and set comparisons
sections.html:
A nested query uses the result of another query. IN tests membership; EXISTS tests whether a subquery returns any row. A correlated subquery refers to attributes of an outer query. The source expresses enrolment in INF-11199 using either IN over student IDs or EXISTS with the correlation S.sid = E.sid.

For a comparison operator op, op ANY requires a true comparison with at least one subquery row; op ALL requires it for every row. IN corresponds to = ANY, and NOT IN to <> ALL. NOT EXISTS tests that no row satisfies the subquery.

SQL predicates can also evaluate to UNKNOWN because of NULL. WHERE retains only TRUE rows. Consequently NOT IN and NOT EXISTS need not behave identically when NULL is possible. On an empty subquery, EXISTS and ANY are false, while NOT EXISTS and ALL are true.

PDF pp. 26–29

quiz.question: In Sale, what is Hue’s total after WHERE amount >= 30?
quiz.explanation: The row with amount=10 is filtered out, leaving 30+90=120. WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY computes SUM, so the sale of 10 does not contribute.
